..
Issued at 130 PM CST Mon Nov 16 2026

Northwesterly flow is found over the northern Plains this 
afternoon as a upper level ridge builds in across the 
southeastern CONUS and as a longwave Pacific trough makes 
landfall across the east. Warm, dry, and mild weather is thus 
expected to persist today and Tuesday under this pattern. With 
very light winds overnight patchy fog is possible across 
portions of western and much of central North Dakota tonight 
through Tuesday morning, though the areal extend of fog will
depend on clearing of the mid and high level clouds anticipated
overnight. Otherwise highs temperatures this afternoon are 
forecast from the 50s to the lower 60s, with low temperatures 
tonight broadly expected to be in the 30s. Quiet weather 
persists through the day Tuesday, with highs expected to broadly
be in the 50s. 

Early Wednesday into Thursday, a robust shortwave impulse 
ejecting out of the Pacific Northwest is progged to cross the 
Rockies, with with lee cyclogenesis spitting a surface low 
pressure system over central Montana. The passage of this low 
pressure system across North Dakota is expected to promote low 
to medium chances across much of the forecast area. The ensemble
favors a northerly track for this system, pushing the axis of 
highest QPF (approaching 0.25") across far northwest North 
Dakota into southern Canada. Light QPF (less than 0.10") can 
still be anticipated elsewhere, though portions of southwestern
and much of south central North Dakota may fall under the dry 
slot. While mainly rain is anticipated with this system, a 
transition to some snowfall is possible across the northwest 
into the north central during the coolest portions Wednesday 
night into Thursday morning. A light dusting of snow is
possible (low chance), mainly across the northwest. This system
also represents a downward turn for temperatures across western
and central North Dakota, with highs dropping back down into 
the 30s west to 40s across the west on Wednesday, then more 
broadly across all of North Dakota on Thursday. Gusty west to 
northwest, sustained around 25 to 35 MPH and gusting as high as 
50 MPH, can also be anticipated the surface pressure gradient 
tightens across the southwest. We will need to monitor this 
period for potential wind headlines, especially if the the 
northward deflection of the system evident in the model trends
continue. 

Chances for precpitation will again increase across the area 
through the day Friday a strong Pacific Northwestern low crosses
over the Rockies and slides across the northern Plains. The 
passage of this system will again spit out a lee side low, this 
time over Wyoming, and loft it across the northern Plains, 
promoting medium to high chances for precipitation across 
portions of North Dakota. Cluster analysis reveals three 
potential scenarios at this time. Scenario one is a well 
dispersed among all model families, and has a plurality of 
ensemble members (approximately 40 percent). In this scenario, 
the well-stacked upper level and surface low is progged to slide
north across South Dakota and eastern North Dakota Friday night
into Saturday, promoting precpitation across much of the 
forecast area. A quick transition from rain into snow early 
Friday night would allow for accumulating snowfall, especially 
across the west and north central. As per this latest forecast 
cycle, low to medium chances for at least 1 inch of snowfall is
anticipated across much of the area, while the southwest has a 
low chance to exceed 2 inches overall. Scenario two is a 
minority cluster (20 percent membership), and shifts the stack 
low further to the southeast. Better gulf moisture returns ahead
of this system would allow for a greater amount of QPF compared
to scenario one while still allowing for the quick transition 
from rain into snow. This would promote a greater (medium to 
high) chance for much of the forecast area to exceed 1 inch of 
snowfall by late Saturday, while western and portions of central
North Dakota would have a low to medium chance to exceed 2 
inches of snowfall through the same period. A third, much less 
impactful scenario is also advertised by a minority (20 percent)
of ensemble members. A comparably weak, open upper level wave 
would be expected to be rapidly displaced east by an building 
upper level ridge off to the west. While some precpitation can 
be anticipated with this scenario the overall transition from 
rain to snow would lag behind the system and thus greatly limit 
overall accumulation, with only a low chance for 1 inch of snow 
across portions of the southwest and central North Dakota. 
Notably, scenarios 2 and 3 are underdispersed, and are 
reflective of the GEPS and the GFS respectively. In either 
scenario cooler weather can be anticipated on the backside of 
this system, with high temperatures broadly expected to be in 
the 30s Sunday heading into early next week.
